title: Slavoj Žižek
keyWorks: Welcome to the Desert of the Real (2002)
summary: Slavoj Žižek is a Slovenian philosopher who brings together Hegel's philosophy, Jacques Lacan's psychoanalysis and the analysis of popular culture. He is known for paradoxical turns of thought, jokes and readings of films. His central theme is ideology: not false ideas in our heads, but the way we live and act even when we "understand everything".
onEmotions: Following Lacan, Žižek holds that our desires and feelings never fully belong to us: we desire through others, through language and shared fantasies. A feeling, for him, is not simply an inner state but the place where our expectations collide with what Lacan called "the Real" — whatever does not fit into our familiar picture of the world. Žižek is suspicious of the culture of obligatory happiness and self-improvement: he calls it the injunction "Enjoy!", which brings more guilt than pleasure. His view is often uncomfortable, but it frees you: you don't need to be whole, and nobody is holding a final answer in reserve.

anxiety.text: Lacan's parable of anxiety, a favorite of Žižek's: you face a giant praying mantis while wearing a mask you can't see, not knowing what it takes you for. Anxiety is heavy, and you needn't shed it at any cost. Žižek, following Lacan, offers an unexpected angle: anxiety arises not when we lack something, but when the lack itself disappears — when what we desire, or other people's expectations, come too close and leave us no room. Lacan said that anxiety, unlike vague unease, does have an object — we just can't see it. Taking Žižek's thought further, your anxiety is not meaningless noise but a signal: something in your life has come right up against you, and you need a little distance. Žižek would remind you that you don't have to know and control everything. Sometimes relief comes when you admit that lack and uncertainty are a normal part of life.
anxiety.practice: Imagine a metre of empty space opening up between you and whatever has come too close — someone's expectation, a question, a desire. Push it back a metre in your mind and take three calm out-breaths.

fear.text: An era in which people are united above all by shared fears — this is how Žižek describes the politics of our day. Your fear, meanwhile, is an ancient protective reaction, and there is nothing shameful in it. In Violence Žižek writes that many social forces now rely on fear — of strangers, of catastrophes, of change — because fear easily unites and controls. Žižek would probably say: some of what we fear has been suggested to us from outside, and it helps to tell your own fear apart from what the culture invites you to be afraid of. Žižek would also remind you that fear often hides a desire: we fear what at the same time attracts us. This view doesn't cancel the fear, but it makes it more understandable — and therefore a little smaller.
fear.practice: Ask yourself out loud: is this fear my own, or did I "pick it up" from the news and the feed? If it's the second, return it to sender with one sentence: "This fear is not mine."

sadness.text: A happy ending hastily glued onto a sad story is something Žižek would call ideology at its purest. Your sadness doesn't need to be hurriedly turned into positivity. Žižek likes to show how the culture of obligatory happiness makes sadness almost forbidden: we are urged to rejoice, to grow, to enjoy life. He calls this the command of the superego — the inner overseer who no longer says "you mustn't" but "enjoy!". When enjoyment becomes a duty, sadness looks like failure. The paradox is that your sadness is a refusal to take part in this show of cheerfulness, and there is honesty in it. It shows that something in your life doesn't fit the smooth picture. Letting yourself be sad means ceasing to obey an impossible order to be happy.
sadness.practice: Look out the window for five minutes without trying to cheer yourself up — as if it were a film with no happy ending. An honest ending is better than a glued-on one.

grief.text: Antigone, burying her brother against the king's ban, is one of Žižek's favorite heroines: an image of faithfulness that can't be revoked. Grief is a deep experience of loss, and it keeps to no timetable. Žižek often turns to Freud's distinction between mourning and melancholia. In mourning a person gradually lets go of what was lost; in melancholia they keep holding on to it. But Žižek, unlike many, sees in melancholia not only an illness: there is fidelity in it, a refusal to betray what was precious. Žižek might add: if you can't "just let go", that isn't necessarily a mistake. Perhaps your grief is keeping something you are not ready to lose a second time. The way forward is not to forget, but to find a form of memory in which what you lost goes on living without taking the present away from you.
grief.practice: Make one small gesture of faithfulness: set on the table something that reminds you of what you lost, or say the name out loud. Faithfulness does not require forgetting.

loneliness.text: Imagine that no one is watching you — not God, not society, not the mysterious "everyone." Žižek says that this is simply the case, and, strangely, the knowledge brings people closer. Loneliness hurts, and it speaks of a deep need for connection. Following Lacan, he repeats that "the big Other does not exist". The "big Other" is an imagined authority that sees everything, understands everything and guarantees meaning: God, society, public opinion. We often feel lonely because it seems that everyone else is connected to this authority and we are not. But for Žižek it doesn't exist for anyone: every person is in some way not fully understood and not fully fitted into the world. Here is what follows: your loneliness is not an exception but a shared human condition. And paradoxically, you can find kinship with others in that.
loneliness.practice: Watch the passers-by — from a window or in the street — and imagine that each of them, too, is not fully understood and not fully at home in the world. Stay for a minute in this strange kinship.

anger.text: "Don't act. Just think" — Žižek threw out this call as a provocation and repeats it again and again. Anger tells you that something has truly touched a nerve. In Violence, Žižek distinguishes visible, "subjective" violence — outbursts, conflicts — from invisible, "objective" violence built into the very system of relations. Anger often reacts to the first, although the cause lies in the second. He believes that a hasty reaction often just reproduces the very thing we are angry about. In other words, your anger doesn't have to turn into action immediately. You can keep it as the energy of understanding: work out what exactly hurt you and where the real source of the problem lies. Then anger becomes not a flare-up but clarity.
anger.practice: Before you act, stop: three slow out-breaths, and then a question to yourself — what am I angry about on the surface, and what lies deeper?

shame.text: Who is the spectator you blush before, even when you are alone in the room? That is exactly what Žižek would ask. Shame is agonizing, and you deserve gentleness towards yourself within it. Žižek, following Lacan, would explain shame through the gaze — more precisely, through the imagined gaze of the "big Other", which seems to see right through us and judge us. We feel ashamed not so much before real people as before this imagined judge. But, as Žižek keeps repeating, the big Other does not exist: there is no all-seeing authority that passes a final verdict. Žižek might go on: your shame rests on a court that doesn't actually exist. Žižek often quotes Beckett: failure is not the end but part of the way. You can allow yourself to be imperfect and carry on — without an all-seeing judge over your head.
shame.practice: Picture the all-seeing judge you feel ashamed before, and describe his appearance to yourself — the robe, the wig, the stern gaze. When he starts to look a little ridiculous, remember: he doesn't exist.

quote.text: Ever tried. Ever failed. No matter. Try again. Fail again. Fail better.
quote.author: Samuel Beckett
quote.source: Worstward Ho (Žižek often quotes these lines)

guilt.text: When you buy coffee at a trendy chain, Žižek says, you also buy absolution: part of the money is promised to those in need. Guilt has become a commodity, but real guilt speaks of your capacity for responsibility, and that is valuable. But Žižek, drawing on Freud, points to a paradox: the superego, the inner overseer, is built so that the more we obey it, the guiltier we feel. Its demands are impossible to meet by definition. Today, according to Žižek, the superego demands not strictness but enjoyment and self-realization: "be happy, be successful, grow!". And we feel guilty for failing at that too. Apply this to yourself, and it turns out that if your guilt is endless, it may come not from a real wrongdoing but from an insatiable inner voice. You can hear it without having to obey it. Real responsibility is concrete; endless guilt is not.
guilt.practice: Ask out loud: if I put right what I did wrong, will the guilt go? If the inner voice immediately finds a new reason, that's the superego, not conscience. Tell it calmly: "Enough."

envy.text: Your neighbor thinks your grass is greener, and you think his is: Žižek turns this old joke into a theory of "stolen enjoyment." Admitting to envy already takes courage. Žižek, following Lacan, holds that desire as such works through others: "desire is the desire of the Other". We want what others want, and what makes others desirable. So envy is not a random vice but the flip side of the very mechanism of desire. Žižek also writes about the fantasy of "stolen enjoyment": it seems to us that others enjoy life more fully than we do, as if they possessed a secret we have been deprived of. It follows that your envy says more about a fantasy than about reality. You can acknowledge that nobody has complete enjoyment — and that takes the edge off the comparison.
envy.practice: Recall one detail of this person's life that you don't actually know but have already sketched in. Erase it in your mind like a stray line, and see what remains.

emptiness.text: The Kinder Surprise egg is one of Žižek's favorite examples: inside there is a void, and in the void a plastic toy, the very reason anyone buys it. A sense of emptiness is hard, and it deserves attention rather than reproach. For Žižek, as for Hegel, the human subject is not a full, whole thing but, at its core, a gap, a void, negativity. Hegel called this "the night of the world". Žižek sees this void not as a defect but as a source of freedom: precisely because we never fully coincide with any single role, we can change and create something new. Žižek would phrase it like this: the emptiness you feel doesn't necessarily mean something is wrong with you. Perhaps it lays bare what has always been at the core of a human being — a space from which something not yet known can emerge.
emptiness.practice: Sit in silence for a minute without filling the emptiness, and ask: if this were not an absence but a free space, what might appear here?

confusion.text: A worker leaving for Siberia agrees with his friends: a letter in blue ink is true, in red ink false. A letter arrives in blue: "Everything is wonderful, only there's no red ink." Žižek tells this joke to show that confusion can be the beginning of thinking. He shows how ideology works not through false ideas but through what seems obvious and natural. We often "know" how the world works, but that knowledge is just a familiar frame. When the frame cracks, confusion appears. For Žižek, this is a valuable moment: you can see that the obvious isn't obvious at all. He notes that sometimes we feel free only because we lack the words to describe our unfreedom. For you this means: confusion is a chance to find those words. There's no need to rush to an answer: a good question is worth more than a quick solution.
confusion.practice: Write down one thing that seemed obvious until recently but no longer does, and turn it into a question. A good question is the red ink you've found.

quote.text: We "feel free" because we lack the very language to articulate our unfreedom.
quote.author: Slavoj Žižek
quote.source: Welcome to the Desert of the Real

fatigue.text: A horseshoe hung over Niels Bohr's door. "You believe in it?" — "No, but they say it works anyway." Žižek loves this story: our race for success works the same way. Your tiredness is real, and it doesn't mean weakness. He describes a phenomenon that, after Octave Mannoni, he calls "fetishistic disavowal": "I know very well, but all the same…". We know very well that the endless race for success and self-improvement wears us out, but all the same we keep taking part in it, as if we didn't know. For Žižek, this is exactly how ideology works: not through ignorance, but through acting against what we know. Seen through Žižek's eyes, your tiredness is the moment when the body stops pretending not to know. It is not defeat but a kind of honesty. You can allow yourself to admit what you have long known — and rest without excuses.
fatigue.practice: Complete the sentence: "I know very well that…, but all the same…". Read it aloud — and give yourself five minutes of rest with no excuses.

quote.text: They know very well what they are doing, but still, they are doing it.
quote.author: Slavoj Žižek

boredom.text: What do decaf coffee and a life without risk have in common? Žižek would answer: both are safe — and therefore bland. Boredom can be unpleasant, and there is nothing shameful in it. He likes to list the products of our time — coffee without caffeine, beer without alcohol, sweets without sugar — and sees in them a symbol of a culture in which everything has had its "dangerous" substance removed. We want experiences, but without risk; relationships, but without upheaval. The conclusion, as so often with Žižek, is unexpected: boredom is the natural result of a "decaf" life, where everything is safe but there is no real intensity. Your boredom may be a healthy signal: you are missing something real, something able to touch you and change you. It is not a complaint but a longing for the real, and it deserves attention.
boredom.practice: Do one thing "with caffeine" today — small but real: strike up a conversation with an unfamiliar shop assistant, take a new route, say out loud something you usually keep to yourself.

joy.text: A good joke only works when you don't see it coming — Žižek, a great lover of jokes, would say joy works the same way. It needs no justification. Žižek could help you tell genuine joy apart from obligatory enjoyment. Lacan used the word jouissance — an "enjoyment" that contains something excessive, even painful. Contemporary culture, according to Žižek, orders us to enjoy, and that turns pleasure into work. But real joy comes unexpectedly — as a gift, not as a completed task. Žižek himself prizes humour and absurdity: in a good joke there is a joy that arises from a gap, from an unexpected twist. Translated into the language of your life, you don't need to "do" joy correctly or hold on to it. It's enough simply to notice it — with laughter and gratitude for its chance nature.
joy.practice: Tell someone a funny little thing from today, or retell a joke that makes you laugh. Joy, like a joke, lives when it is told.

love.text: Žižek, in a documentary, provocatively calls love evil: it picks one person out of billions for no rational reason and sets them above everyone else. The tenderness you feel is among the deepest human experiences. Love, in his view, is not choosing the best option from a list of qualities but a fall: we love a person not for their merits, but together with their imperfections, and even through them. Žižek also sees love as an event — something that breaks the habitual course of life. Žižek might put it this way: your tenderness is neither weakness nor illusion, but a rare moment when you step beyond calculation. You can accept it with all its imperfect, unreasonable strength.
love.practice: Name one "imperfect" trait of the person you love that is dearer to you than any virtue — and, if you like, tell them so.

gratitude.text: The world never promised anyone anything — it sounds grim, but Žižek would draw an unexpectedly warm conclusion from it. Gratitude is a feeling that connects you with the world and with other people. If, as he repeats after Lacan, "the big Other does not exist" and nobody guarantees us meaning or good fortune, then everything good in life is not an owed reward but a chance that might never have happened. That makes gratitude deeper: you are grateful not to a system that "owes" you something, but to a fragile coincidence of circumstances and to particular people. This view removes the expectation that the world is obliged to be fair, and lets you be surprised by the good. Gratitude becomes not a duty but wonder.
gratitude.practice: Pick one good thing in your life and for a minute imagine a world without it. Then come back to this, the real one, and notice how it shines.

hope.text: The light at the end of the tunnel may be an oncoming train — Žižek repeats this old joke with evident pleasure. And yet hope matters, and it's good that you have it. Žižek's relation to hope is complicated. In The Courage of Hopelessness, following Giorgio Agamben, he criticizes easy, soothing hope — the kind that tells you to wait as if everything will sort itself out. But his conclusion is not gloomy: giving up false guarantees opens a space for real action. When we stop waiting for someone to come and fix everything, we gain the possibility of starting change ourselves. Followed to the end, this thought means that your hope grows stronger when it doesn't rest on illusions. It may sound not like "everything will definitely be fine" but like "I don't know how it will turn out, but I can take my own small step".
hope.practice: Say your hope out loud in two versions — "let … happen" and "I can do …". Spend at least five minutes on what you heard in the second.

nostalgia.text: Titanic, for Žižek, is a story of how an iceberg saved the lovers from the future: had they reached shore, their romance would hardly have lasted a year. Loss kept the fantasy intact. Nostalgia is a warm, aching feeling. Žižek, following Lacan, speaks of the "objet a" — the object-cause of desire, which we experience as lost even though we never possessed it in full. The loss itself creates its value. The simple conclusion: the past you miss glows partly because it is gone — and memory tints it in colours that may not have been there at the time. That doesn't make your nostalgia false. On the contrary, it shows what you truly desire. Žižek would suggest asking: what exactly in the past is dear to you? Perhaps it can be found not only in memory but in the present too.
nostalgia.practice: Put on a song from that time and ask: do I miss the place and the time — or the feeling I had then? Then look for that feeling somewhere today.

craving.text: Coca-Cola was once sold as "the real thing," and Žižek notes that's exactly why it's never enough: the more you drink, the thirstier you get. A sharp "I want it now" can be very strong, and it's nothing to be ashamed of. Žižek, following Lacan, would offer an unusual view. The thing you want — a cigarette, a glass, your phone — only temporarily occupies the place of what Lacan called the "objet a", the elusive cause of desire. That is why, having got what we wanted, we so often feel: "that's not it". Žižek would likely note: a craving promises a fullness no thing can give — and the problem is not your weakness but the very nature of desire. Knowing this doesn't cancel the wave, but it changes how you relate to it: you have every right not to believe its promise. The wave rises and falls even if you don't feed it.
craving.practice: When the craving comes, rest a palm on your chest and ask it: "What exactly are you promising me — calm, joy, oblivion?" Breathe for three minutes, watching how both the promise and the wave change.

addiction.text: Lacan pictured the drive as an arrow that circles its target and returns to the archer — Žižek uses this to explain why the circuit itself holds us. If life has long revolved around something hard to leave, that is hard, and not a moral failure. Žižek, drawing on Lacan, distinguishes desire from drive. Desire seeks an object and is always disappointed; drive, by contrast, finds satisfaction in the circuit itself, in repetition. Lacan called this peculiar, almost painful pleasure jouissance. Taking Žižek's thought further, an addiction holds on not because the substance or habit is so very pleasant, but because the repeating circuit itself has become a support, a way of organizing life. This explains why willpower alone is so often not enough — and it lifts the shame. Žižek would remind you that the way out is not to become "perfect" but to find another support, another form around which a life can be built.
addiction.practice: Ask yourself, as Žižek would: "What does this circuit give my life — shape, rhythm, shelter? What else could my day circle around?" If you want, you can talk about it with people who know this path from the inside, for example in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: First the superego commands "Enjoy!", and the next morning it punishes you for obeying — Žižek loves exposing this double game. The morning after — with a headache, anxiety, shame and gaps in memory — is hard, and you deserve gentleness, not judgment. The paradox of the superego, for Žižek, is that the more you obey it, the stronger the guilt. Žižek would probably say: the moral hangover is not the voice of truth about you, but the work of this cruel authority, which can never be satisfied. You don't have to pass sentence on yourself. You can notice the guilt without agreeing with its conclusions, and simply take care of yourself today.
hangover.practice: Say this morning's loudest accusing thought out loud, then answer it: "This is the voice of the superego, not the final truth about me." Open a window and breathe.

euphoria.text: "Carnivals come cheap. What matters is the day after," Žižek told the protesters on Wall Street in 2011. You can live this bright flash with pleasure — the only question is what you will take away with you. The paradox is that euphoria is valuable, but the real question is not how to hold on to it but what you can take with you from it. This view doesn't spoil the high — it protects it: you don't demand that it last forever, you let it be what it is. And you know in advance that ordinary life afterwards is not a defeat but a place where you can bring what opened up.
euphoria.practice: Pick one small thing from this high to take into tomorrow's ordinary day — a phrase, a song, a gesture — and decide exactly where it will come in handy.

crash.text: What remains of a party once the guests have gone? Žižek considers this the most interesting question. And the drop after a high can be very hard: the colours drain away, and it seems it will always be like this. Žižek often talks about "the day after" — the moment after a celebration, a revolution, a big event, when you have to return to ordinary life. For him this is not a defeat but the most interesting part: that is when it becomes clear what has really changed. Žižek might add: the comedown is not a refutation of the high but its second half. Žižek's Lacanian view adds that no enjoyment can last without turning into its opposite. The drop is not proof that the good was a lie. It is simply a time when you are back on the ground and can calmly look at what has stayed with you.
crash.practice: Walk for five minutes and gather along the way three things that stayed with you after the high — however small: a new acquaintance, a thought, a memory.

panic.text: Words are the handrail the psyche holds on to — a simplified version of Žižek's thought about the Real. When panic hits — heart pounding, short of air, as if something irreparable is about to happen — it is very hard, and you are not alone. Žižek, following Lacan, speaks of "the Real" — what breaks through our familiar picture of the world and can't be put into words. Panic resembles such a breakthrough: meanings and footholds vanish for a moment, and only bare experience remains. Here is what follows: one remedy against the Real is language: naming, returning to the symbolic. Right now, in the middle of the wave, philosophy is not the main thing. The main thing is that the wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Naming the things around you is a simple way to lean on the world again.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and make each out-breath longer than the in-breath. Name five things around you out loud in full — "grey mug," "wooden table" — holding on to the words like a handrail.

dread.text: "The night of the world" — the young Hegel's name for the abyss inside us, and Žižek returns to it again and again. The question "what is it all for?", the sense of an abyss, is among the deepest human experiences, and it doesn't make you weaker. Žižek wouldn't comfort you with simple answers, but his view can be unexpectedly supportive. Following Hegel, he holds that at the core of a human being lies negativity — a void, a gap, the absence of ready-made meaning. For Žižek this is not a catastrophe but the condition of freedom: if meaning were given in advance, we would be mere mechanisms. Lacan said that "the big Other does not exist" — there is no authority guaranteeing that everything is right. In other words, the abyss you feel is also a space in which people create meaning themselves, together with others, step by step.
dread.practice: Do one small thing today that has meaning precisely for you — water a plant, call a friend, finish a page. Let meaning be made rather than found.

fomo.text: Somewhere, it seems, the real party is going on, while you sit in the kitchen with the kettle; Žižek would say that party exists only in fantasy. The feeling that others live more interesting lives is very common, and there is nothing shameful in it. Žižek, following Lacan, speaks of the fantasy of "the enjoyment of the Other": it seems to us that somewhere other people are enjoying life more fully, more deeply, for real, and we are deprived of it. This fantasy is almost always exaggerated — after all, those we envy feel the same way about someone else. Žižek might go on: the fear of missing out is not information about where things are actually good but the structure of desire itself. Nobody is in "the place to be". This knowledge frees you: you can stop chasing an imaginary centre of life and notice what is happening here.
fomo.practice: In your mind, peek into that "real party" you're missing. Most likely someone there is also standing by the wall, thinking the real party is somewhere else.

sleepless.text: We wake up not because of reality but to escape into it — one of the most unexpected paradoxes Žižek takes from Lacan. Insomnia with thoughts going in circles is exhausting, and it is not your fault. Žižek often recalls a dream analysed by Freud: a father dreams of his child who has burned, and he wakes up to escape what he encountered in the dream. Apply this to yourself, and it turns out that at night, when the day's tasks and roles recede, what we have been putting off comes closer. Night thoughts seem final, but they are not — they are what awaits calm attention in daylight. You don't have to solve everything now. You can simply admit, "yes, this worries me", and put off the answer until morning.
sleepless.practice: Whisper to yourself: "Yes, this worries me — I'll deal with it in the morning." Then breathe slowly, counting your out-breaths from ten down to one.

betrayal.text: "The neighbour," for Žižek, is not a nice person next door but an abyss: there is always something in the closest person that we cannot know. That is why betrayal wounds so deeply: a bond collapses, along with the belief that you can rely on another. Betrayal is the moment when that abyss suddenly opens. It follows that your pain doesn't mean you were foolish or blind. No one can fully know another; all trust is a wager, not a calculation. Žižek doesn't suggest giving up trust; he suggests acknowledging its fragility. Your capacity to take risks for the sake of closeness is not a mistake — it is what makes love and friendship possible.
betrayal.practice: Write two lines: "What this betrayal says about the other person" and "What it says nothing about in me."

jealousy.text: Jalouissance — Lacan glued this word together from "jealousy" and "enjoyment," and Žižek uses it readily. Jealousy is agonizing and very human; you don't need to shame yourself for it. Žižek develops the thought: jealousy is often tied to a fantasy about the enjoyment of the Other — that the rival, or the loved one themselves, is getting something we are deprived of. We suffer not only from what is happening but also from what we fill in ourselves. Žižek would phrase it like this: jealousy often paints pictures more vivid than reality. That doesn't mean your fear is unfounded — but it helps to tell what you know apart from what you imagine. Making that distinction gives you back a little freedom.
jealousy.practice: Divide a page into two columns: "what I know for sure" and "what I'm filling in." See which is longer.

resentment.text: A sore tooth you keep touching with your tongue — Žižek would probably recognize in this gesture the hidden enjoyment of a grievance. An old grievance is a weight, and often there is a real injustice behind it that deserves acknowledgement. Žižek would ask an unexpected question: could it be that the grievance itself is holding us? From a Lacanian point of view there may be a hidden "enjoyment" in it — jouissance: we replay the scene again and again, and in that painful repetition there is something hard to give up. This is not a reproach, nor a reason for shame — many human feelings work this way. For you this means: noticing this circuit is the first step towards freedom from it. Letting go of a grievance doesn't necessarily mean forgiving or excusing; it means reclaiming the energy that goes into repeating the past.
resentment.practice: Each time your mind returns to this story, gently note to yourself: "the circuit again" — and shift your attention to something nearby: a sound, the light, an object.

heartbreak.text: "I've fallen in love" is, for Žižek as for Badiou, not a state but an event after which the world is no longer the same. That is why a broken heart really hurts, and it needs time. We love not an ideal image but a particular person — with all their imperfections. That is why a breakup destroys not just a relationship but a whole world that grew up around that encounter. Seen through Žižek's eyes, your pain is in proportion to how deeply you were touched. It is not a sign of weakness but the trace of a real event. Žižek doesn't promise quick comfort, but the very capacity to love like this and to lose like this remains yours — it doesn't leave with the other person.
heartbreak.practice: Write one sentence about what this love changed in you — what you learned about yourself and the world through it.

impostor.text: In Kung Fu Panda the Dragon Scroll turns out to be a blank mirror: there is no secret ingredient. Žižek loves the cartoon for exactly this twist. The fear that you are about to be found out says nothing about your real worth. Žižek, following Lacan, speaks of the "symbolic mandate": a title, a post, a role is something society gives us, not a natural property. A judge is a judge not because there is some judge-essence "inside" him, but because he has been invested with that place. The conclusion, as so often with Žižek, is unexpected: in a sense everyone is a bit of an "impostor" — there is always a gap between a person and their role. Those who don't feel it are not more genuine; they simply notice the gap less. Your feeling is not an exposure but honesty. You can perform a role without being it entirely.
impostor.practice: Remind yourself aloud: "My role is …, and I am more than this role." No one has a secret ingredient, so you don't need to look for yours.

quote.text: If a man who thinks he is a king is mad, a king who thinks he is a king is no less so.
quote.author: Jacques Lacan
quote.source: "Presentation on Psychical Causality" (Žižek often cites this idea)

self_hatred.text: A judge who never acquits is not justice but mockery — roughly how Žižek speaks of our inner critic. If your inner voice is merciless, that is very hard, and its verdicts are not the truth about you. Žižek, following Freud and Lacan, explains why this voice is so cruel. The superego — the inner critic — is built paradoxically: the harder we try to please it, the stricter it becomes. Žižek calls this authority "obscene": it is not a fair judge but an insatiable overseer who will never say "enough". Translated into the language of your life, the cruelty of the inner critic is not proof of your guilt but a feature of the mechanism itself. So it is pointless trying to become so good that it falls silent. You can only learn not to take it at its word, and to listen to other voices — fairer and kinder ones.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one sentence from your inner critic and answer it in Žižek's spirit, with irony: "Thank you, superego, as always it's not enough for you." Read your answer aloud.

helplessness.text: "I would prefer not to," Melville's Bartleby answered everything, and Žižek sees unexpected strength in that quiet refusal. Helplessness is heavy, especially when nothing seems changeable, and it deserves compassion. Žižek is known for a provocative piece of advice: sometimes, when everyone demands immediate action, it is better to stop and think. He observed that frantic activity often just sustains what we would like to change. Žižek might put it this way: your powerlessness is not necessarily a defeat. Perhaps it is a pause in which old ways of acting have stopped working and new ones have not yet been found. Žižek also reminds us that "the big Other does not exist": there is no all-seeing authority that has already decided nothing will change. The future is not predetermined, and there is room for hope in that. The first step might be not a leap but a clear question.
helplessness.practice: Sit for five minutes doing nothing, like Bartleby — not out of powerlessness but in order to think. Then ask yourself one clear question: what can I at least understand?

procrastination.text: "Try again. Fail again. Fail better" — Žižek quotes these words of Beckett's so often that they have almost become his motto. "I can't get started" is not laziness or a flaw of character. Desire, for Lacan, is sustained by lack: as long as a task hasn't been started, it stays ideal, full of possibilities. Starting means facing an imperfect result, and the fear of that can hold us back. Followed to the end, this thought means that putting things off protects the dream of flawless execution. Beckett's formula takes the pressure off: nobody expects a perfect start from you. The first step can be clumsy — and that is exactly why it is real. Sometimes it's enough to allow yourself to do it badly in order to start at all.
procrastination.practice: Allow yourself to do the first five minutes of work deliberately "badly" — a draft, a sketch, a crooked first line. Fail better.

uprooted.text: The country Žižek grew up in is no longer on the map: Yugoslavia vanished, and he knows well how a familiar world disappears. Being torn away from home affects a person deeply, and your sense of loss is legitimate. His philosophy offers an unexpected view. Following Hegel and Lacan, he holds that a human being is, in principle, never entirely "at home" — not even in their own culture, not even in themselves. In each of us there is a gap, a foreignness. The simple conclusion: emigration makes visible what was always there — and that knowledge can set you free. Žižek also sees a special possibility in the position of someone "not quite one of us": an outside view lets you notice what locals don't see. Your uprootedness is both a loss and a new point of view.
uprooted.practice: Walk around your new place like an anthropologist from another country and notice one oddity the locals stopped seeing long ago. The outsider's eye is your advantage.

overload.text: In the film They Live the hero puts on dark glasses and sees the real orders on the billboards: "Consume," "Obey" — Žižek adores this scene. Overload from the endless flood of news and messages is real exhaustion. Žižek observed that in today's world we are offered endless choice and endless information, but this doesn't make us freer: the more options there are, the heavier the burden of decisions and the stronger the anxiety that we've missed something. Following Lacan, he says that "the big Other does not exist" — there is no authority that knows everything and keeps track of it all. Žižek would likely note: you don't need to be that all-knowing authority. Nobody knows everything; nobody has read the whole feed. Letting go of complete information is not irresponsibility but an acknowledgement that you are human.
overload.practice: Choose one topic you follow out of habit and allow yourself to know nothing about it until the end of the week. No one has ever read the whole feed.

unreality.text: "I want a third pill," Žižek says of The Matrix — not red or blue, but one showing the reality within the illusion. When everything, or you yourself, seems unreal, it is strange and unsettling and deserves gentle treatment. Žižek thought a great deal about the nature of reality. Following Lacan, he holds that what we experience as "reality" always rests on an invisible frame — language, habits, the fantasy that gives the world its coherence. In Welcome to the Desert of the Real he discusses how, in The Matrix, the hero discovers that the familiar world was just a picture. Taking Žižek's thought further, the feeling of unreality can arise when this frame temporarily loosens and the world loses its usual density. That doesn't mean "something is wrong" with you. The frame comes back, especially if you gently lean on simple things and sensations.
unreality.practice: Touch something nearby and name three of its qualities out loud — "cold, smooth, heavy": let language make the world solid again.

awe.text: Žižek called his first major book in English The Sublime Object of Ideology — the sublime fascinated him from the start. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare experience, worth savouring fully. Žižek, following Kant and Lacan, thought a lot about the sublime. Lacan defined sublimation as raising an object to the dignity of the Thing: an ordinary thing suddenly begins to glow with something greater than itself. Žižek would probably say: awe is a moment when the world briefly goes beyond the familiar and the useful and becomes something inexpressibly large. There is nothing naive about it. It is a reminder that reality is not exhausted by what we know about it. Such an experience doesn't need to be explained right away — you can simply live it.
awe.practice: Stay one more minute with what filled you with awe, and don't look for words — just look or listen.

relief.text: The exam is over, and the catastrophe you expected never came: Žižek would say that in this moment you caught the "big Other" in the act of not existing. Something heavy has let go, and it is a warm, well-earned feeling. Žižek would probably notice something important in relief. Often what weighs on us is not the situation itself but an imagined gaze — that of what Lacan called the "big Other": an all-seeing judge to whom we are constantly accountable. Relief sometimes comes when that gaze weakens for a moment: it turns out that nobody expected the impossible from you, that the catastrophe didn't happen. The paradox is that relief is a small discovery that "the big Other does not exist". The world is not as strict as we thought. This moment is worth remembering — it may come in handy next time the pressure returns.
relief.practice: Note down one sentence: "I was afraid that…, but in fact…" — your small proof that "the big Other does not exist." Keep it for the future.

calm.text: "Tarrying with the negative" — Žižek took this phrase of Hegel's as the title of one of his books. Your calm is a precious state, and you can simply enjoy it. Žižek is suspicious of calm that becomes an escape from the world: he criticized the fashion for "Western Buddhism", which helps us take part calmly in the frantic race without changing anything in it. But he values a different calm — the one Hegel spoke of when he wrote about "tarrying with the negative". This is not the absence of contradictions but the ability to bear them calmly without demanding final harmony from life. Žižek might add: your calm doesn't have to be perfect or everlasting. It can live alongside the unfinished and the imperfect — and that is exactly why it can be real. You can simply stay in it.
calm.practice: Sit still for a minute and silently name one contradiction in your life that is still unresolved. Stay with it calmly, as Hegel advised — without resolving it.

inspiration.text: An idea that seems to come out of nowhere is, for Žižek, an event in miniature. Inspiration is a lively, joyful feeling, and it's worth greeting with gratitude. Žižek speaks a lot about the "event" — something that arises unexpectedly and changes the frame through which we see the world. Žižek values such moments, but warns against two traps: expecting complete perfection from an idea, and being afraid of failure. He often quotes Beckett: "Fail again. Fail better." Here is what follows: inspiration doesn't have to become a flawless result straight away. What matters more is that it has opened a new possibility. You can let it unfold without being frightened that the first attempts will be imperfect.
inspiration.practice: Write down the idea in its rawest form, correcting nothing, and add one small action to start trying it out.

schadenfreude.text: "Take out one of my eyes!" — so ends an old joke Žižek retells again and again. Schadenfreude is unpleasant to notice in yourself, but this joke reveals a lot about the nature of desire. A witch offers a peasant: "I will grant any wish of yours, but I'll do the same to your neighbour twice over." The peasant thinks, then asks to be deprived of something, just so his neighbour gets it twice as bad. The point is that our pleasure, according to Lacan, is often linked not to what we have but to what the other lacks. Žižek sees in this an envy built into desire itself. In other words, schadenfreude is not your personal corruption but a universal human mechanism. Once you notice it, you can smile at yourself as at the hero of the joke — and in doing so already slip a little out of its grip.
schadenfreude.practice: When you notice schadenfreude, retell yourself the joke about the witch and the peasant, and ask: what do I actually want for myself, rather than against someone else?

contempt.text: Hegel's "beautiful soul" stands above the corrupt world and condemns it, not noticing that it lives in that world and even needs it to remain a judge; Žižek often recalls this figure. Contempt gives you a pleasant feeling of purity: I am not like them. For Žižek this is not an accusation but a description of a trap everyone falls into. Žižek might go on: contempt often protects us from an uncomfortable question: what role do I myself play in what I despise? Asking it doesn't mean giving up judgment: you can still consider someone's behaviour unacceptable. But contempt will give way to a clearer, calmer view — without the pedestal, on which it is very lonely to stand.
contempt.practice: In your mind, step down from the pedestal: stand beside the person you despise and ask yourself what role you yourself play in what outrages you.

disgust.text: German, French and American toilets are built differently, and Žižek gleefully derives three ideologies from this: even squeamishness speaks of a culture. Disgust is a strong, almost bodily feeling, aimed at people, situations, even yourself. Žižek, following Lacan, observes that what disgusts us is often not the person as such but their "enjoyment" — the way they eat, laugh, live, smell, everything that seems both foreign and too close. Lacan coined a word for this intimate foreignness: "extimacy". Žižek shows that many prejudices are built on this: it seems to us that another's enjoyment threatens our own. Apply this to yourself, and it turns out that disgust says more about us — about our boundaries and fears — than about what caused it. And if it is turned towards yourself, that too is "extimate": everyone has something in them that feels alien — that is how every person is made.
disgust.practice: Name out loud what exactly disgusts you: the person as such, or the way they enjoy life. Just notice the difference.

revenge.text: In fantasy, revenge is perfect: the offender understands, repents and admits you were right. Žižek would look at this scene more closely. The wish for revenge is understandable: you were hurt and want the other to feel the same. Žižek, drawing on psychoanalysis, writes a great deal about "fantasy" — the inner scene that gives shape to our desire. Revenge fantasies often bring relief precisely as fantasies: in them we regain the power we lacked at the moment of the injury. Žižek stresses that fantasy and action are fundamentally different things, and notes that directly realizing a fantasy usually turns out to be a nightmare, not a satisfaction. It follows that the wish for revenge doesn't make you a bad person. You can ask your fantasy: what is the main thing in it — that the offender should hurt, or that it should finally be acknowledged that you were treated unjustly?
revenge.practice: Follow your revenge fantasy to the moment the offender finally understands. What do you feel in that second? Think about where else you could get that recognition — safely for everyone.

anger_at_loved.text: "Love thy neighbour" — Žižek notes this is hardest with those closest to us: up close, the other is unpredictable. Anger at loved ones feels especially shameful. Žižek, following Freud and Lacan, writes a lot about "the neighbour" and observes that the closest person remains at the same time an enigma: there is always something unpredictable and impenetrable in them. Closeness doesn't make the other transparent — on the contrary, it is up close that we run into their incomprehensible desires, habits and demands. Žižek would phrase it like this: anger at a partner, parent or child is a natural response to this too-intimate encounter with another, not proof of a lack of love. There's no need to unload it on the person you love, but there's no need to consider yourself a monster either. Sometimes a little distance is enough to see the person in your loved one again.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger rises, step out for five minutes into another room or outside — let "the neighbour" become a little more distant again. When you come back, ask: what was I expecting from them just now?

ambivalence.text: Hainamoration — Lacan glued this word together from the French haine ("hatred") and enamoration ("falling in love"), and Žižek often uses it. Loving someone and not being able to stand them at the same time is not a malfunction but the most ordinary structure of a strong attachment. Žižek shows more than once that wherever we are deeply involved, opposing feelings inevitably arise: the other means so much to us that their imperfection wounds us all the more. He is sceptical of the ideal of "pure" love without contradictions. For you this means: your ambivalence is a sign of a real bond, not its absence. You don't have to choose which of the feelings is true. Both are true, and admitting that is already a relief.
ambivalence.practice: Say to yourself in one sentence: "I love you — and it annoys me that…". Don't choose between the two halves: Lacan has a whole word for this.

guilty_relief.text: "You didn't do enough" — Žižek calls this voice not conscience but the superego, an insatiable overseer you don't have to believe. Relief you feel ashamed of — after a breakup, after someone leaves, even after the death of a seriously ill loved one — often comes with heavy guilt. Žižek, following Freud and Lacan, explains guilt through the "superego" — an inner authority that, paradoxically, becomes stricter the harder we try to live up to it. You can care for someone for years and still feel you didn't do enough. Seen through Žižek's eyes, your guilt is this authority at work, not a just verdict. Relief, meanwhile, is the honest response of body and soul to the end of a long strain. Love and relief can live side by side.
guilty_relief.practice: Imagine a friend telling you this story, and listen to what your kindest voice would answer. Say the same thing to yourself.

indifference.text: A Tibetan prayer wheel prays for you while you spin it — Žižek calls this "interpassivity": we often hand our feelings over to someone or something else. When something that "should" move you doesn't, it is frightening. The canned laughter in sitcoms laughs for us; in some cultures, at funerals, professional mourners weep in place of the relatives. Žižek sees in this not hypocrisy but a deep feature of being human: feelings don't have to unfold fully "inside" at the right moment. A ritual, a form, a gesture can carry them for us. The conclusion, as so often with Žižek, is unexpected: your indifference doesn't cancel your connection to what is happening. The feeling may come later, differently, at an unexpected moment — or be expressed in an action rather than an experience.
indifference.practice: If the feeling doesn't come, make one small gesture that expresses it — send a word of support, light a candle. That is enough.

escape.text: An island where all will be different helps us bear the mainland: Žižek views escape fantasies with interest and irony. The wish to drop everything — job, city, role — comes to many. He notes that the fantasy of an "elsewhere" where everything will be different often helps us bear the present — and at the same time lets us change nothing in it. Yet he also values the genuine "act" — a deed that changes the very frame of a situation. Translated into the language of your life, your wish to escape says that the current frame has become too tight. It matters to understand what exactly you want to leave behind: a place, or the rules you live by. Sometimes the frame can be changed without going anywhere; sometimes a move is needed. You don't have to decide right away — first it is worth hearing what this wish is telling you.
escape.practice: Finish this sentence: "Where I want to run to, I wouldn't have to…". Then think which of these rules you could break right here, without going anywhere — that would be a small "act."

forbidden_attraction.text: Forbidden fruit is sweet not despite the ban but because of it — Žižek takes this old wisdom seriously. Being attracted to someone who is "off-limits" can be unsettling. Žižek often quotes the apostle Paul: "I had not known sin, but by the law." For him this is a key to how desire works: a prohibition doesn't only restrain desire, it partly generates it, making the object especially alluring. Lacan said that our desire is always bound up with the Other: we want what is marked by someone else's gaze, by a prohibition, by inaccessibility. Žižek might put it this way: the strength of your attraction has a lot to do with the "forbiddenness" itself, not only with the person. That's no reason for shame. You can look with curiosity at what in this attraction belongs to the person, and what belongs to the inaccessibility itself.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Try a thought experiment: imagine this person became fully available and "allowed." What happens to the attraction? Just watch how the law acts on it.

quote.text: Man's desire is the desire of the Other.
quote.author: Jacques Lacan
quote.source: Seminar XI, The Four Fundamental Concepts of Psychoanalysis (Žižek often cites this formula)

social_anxiety.text: A man who thought he was a grain of seed is cured — and still flees a chicken: one of Žižek's favorite jokes. Fear of people's judgment can likewise turn a simple meeting into an ordeal. After treatment the grain-man understood that he was a man, not a grain — but on going outside he ran back in terror: there's a chicken out there! "I know I'm not a grain," he explains. "But does the chicken know?" Žižek uses this story to show that convincing yourself is not enough, because what troubles us is the imagined "big Other" — what we believe everyone thinks. Followed to the end, this thought means that you can know that you're fine and still be afraid of other people's gaze; that's not stupidity but how the psyche is built. And remember: this all-seeing assessor is a fantasy, and real people are mostly busy with themselves.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, ask yourself with a smile: "But does the chicken know?" — and at the meeting itself, notice who is actually looking at you. Most often, no one.

uncertainty.text: A forecast, a horoscope, "experts say" — we seek someone who knows for sure; Žižek replies that no one has such a knower. Uncertainty is unsettling: you want a guarantee that all will be well. Žižek speaks about this through a formula he repeats after Lacan: "the big Other does not exist". It means there is no higher authority — not in society, not in history — that knows in advance how everything will turn out and keeps a plan ready. At first glance this is frightening. But for Žižek it is also a liberation: if the future isn't written in advance, there is room in it for the unexpected, for what he calls an "event". The simple conclusion: uncertainty is not only emptiness but openness. You don't have to fill it with fantasies of the worst. You can admit "I don't know" — and leave room in that not-knowing for good things too.
uncertainty.practice: Imagine the worst-case scenario, and next to it one unexpectedly good one, and hold them side by side in your mind for a minute. Both are equally unknown so far.

waiting.text: A man waits his whole life at the door of the Law, and at the end learns that this door was meant only for him — Žižek returns to Kafka's parable again and again. Waiting for an answer, a result, news can be more draining than the news itself. Žižek sees here how waiting itself becomes a trap: we grant those we are waiting to hear from enormous power over our lives. Žižek would likely note: while you wait, it is easy to give all your time to what is being decided behind a closed door. Your agitation is natural — the answer really does matter. But life isn't only on the other side of the door. Part of it is right here, in this hour of waiting, which belongs to you too.
waiting.practice: Pick one thing you've put off "until the answer comes" and do it today. Life is not only on the other side of the door.

regret.text: When Caesar crossed the Rubicon, it was just crossing a small river; what happened afterwards made it a great act. Regret over what you did or didn't do makes you replay the past again and again. Žižek, drawing on Hegel, talks a lot about "retroactivity": the meaning of an event is determined not at the moment it happens but after the fact — by what happens next. The past, for Žižek, can't be changed factually, but its meaning can. A mistake can retroactively become a turning point, the beginning of something important — depending on what you do next. Taking Žižek's thought further, your regret is not a final verdict. The story in which this mistake happened is not finished yet, and the next chapter can change the meaning of the earlier ones.
regret.practice: Complete the sentence: "A year from now I may remember this as the moment when…". Come up with at least one version: the meaning of the past is still being written.

longing.text: "Coffee without cream, please." — "We're out of cream; can I bring you coffee without milk?" Žižek adores this joke from a Lubitsch film: absences differ. Missing a particular person is one of the strongest feelings there is. Žižek, following Lacan, says that in the person we love we love something elusive — the "objet petit a", that special, unrepeatable something you can't point your finger at but that makes this person the only one. No one else can replace them, because this "something" can't be reduced to qualities you could list. Žižek would probably say: your longing is so strong precisely because what you miss is not "someone" but this very person. It is a sign of genuine attachment. You don't have to drive the longing away. You can let it be — as a testimony to how special this person has become to you.
longing.practice: Try to describe out loud the elusive something that only this person has. Notice how words fall short — that is exactly what you miss.

world_pain.text: "False urgency" is Žižek's name for the feeling a stream of shocking images creates: be horrified at once, do something at once, before you've had time to think. Pain for the world — wars, injustice, people's suffering — can be enormous. In Violence, Žižek distinguishes "subjective" violence, which we see in the news, from "objective" violence, built into the way the world is arranged and therefore almost invisible. Žižek suggests something else — to stop and think. The paradox is that your pain is a legitimate response, not a weakness. But you are not obliged to live through every new horror in real time. A step back is not indifference but a way to preserve your strength and clarity so that you can understand what is happening more deeply.
world_pain.practice: Instead of one more news feed, read one calm, thoughtful piece about what troubles you. Then sit in silence for a minute.

rejection.text: "Che vuoi?" — "What do you want?" — for Lacan this is the question we always ask the other, and Žižek often returns to it. Rejection hurts: it seems as if someone has spotted something "wrong" in you and passed judgment. Žižek, following Lacan, would remind you that we never fully know what the other wants — and often the other doesn't know either. The other's desire is opaque, so any refusal is not a precise measurement of your worth but the result of a tangled play of someone else's desires, fears and circumstances. Žižek might add: rejection speaks of an encounter between two opaque people, not of a flaw in you. The pain of it is real and worth acknowledging. But the conclusion "something is wrong with me" is your interpretation, not a fact.
rejection.practice: Come up with two explanations for this refusal that have nothing to do with your flaws — just as plausible as your first one.

abandonment.text: Lacan wrote the "Other" with a capital letter and struck it through; for Žižek this means that even the person who matters most is not all-powerful. The fear of being abandoned is deep, often from childhood, and deserves gentleness. Žižek, following Lacan, speaks of the "barred Other": the other person is neither all-powerful nor whole; they have their own fears, doubts and lacks. When we fear being left, we unwittingly imagine the other as a confident master of the situation who could walk away at will at any moment. But most often they are afraid too — of not being enough, of being rejected. Here is what follows: your fear is not a prophecy but a response to the unavoidable uncertainty of any living bond. Knowing that the other is just as vulnerable, you can speak your fear aloud — and then it stops being a secret that eats away at you from within.
abandonment.practice: At a calm moment, ask the person close to you: "And what are you afraid of in our relationship?" — and simply listen to the answer.

unrequited.text: "To love is to give what you don't have" — Žižek repeats this enigmatic formula of Lacan's again and again. Unrequited love is a feeling with nowhere to go, and it hurts. Love, in this view, is not an exchange of values or a deal in which an investment is owed a return. It is the gift of one's own lack, an openness that can never be guaranteed. That is why love is always risky: the other may not respond, and no merits can change that. In other words, the lack of a response doesn't make your feeling a mistake or a weakness, and it is no measure of your worth. You dared to do the riskiest thing a human being is capable of. The pain of it is real — but so is your courage.
unrequited.practice: Tell yourself out loud: "I dared to love without knowing what would happen, and that was brave."

quote.text: Love is giving what you don't have.
quote.author: Jacques Lacan
quote.source: Seminar VIII, Transference (Žižek often cites this formula)

humiliation.text: "A madman who thinks he is a king is no madder than a king who thinks he is a king" — Žižek loves this line of Lacan's. Humiliation feels as though something very important has been torn off you, and everyone saw it. Žižek, following Lacan, distinguishes a person from their "symbolic mandate" — their role, status, place in others' eyes: manager, specialist, respected member of the family. Humiliation strikes precisely at the mandate — at how you are seen — and that is why it feels like a catastrophe. But Žižek reminds us that we never fully coincide with our role; there is always a gap between a person and their title. Žižek might go on: what has been hit is your symbolic position, not who you are. A position can be restored or changed, and you are more than any of them. And in that gap your dignity remains.
humiliation.practice: Write down which of your roles the humiliation struck, and next to it — three things about yourself that depend on no role at all.

body_shame.text: In Hitchcock's Vertigo, Scottie remakes Judy until she resembles the lost Madeleine — for Žižek, an image of seeing ourselves through another's eyes. Being unhappy with your body is rarely about the body alone. Žižek, drawing on Lacan, distinguishes the "ideal ego" — the image of how we would like to look — from the "ego ideal" — the imagined point from which we are judged and whose approval we strive for. Dissatisfaction with the body is often born not from the reflection itself but from looking at ourselves through the eyes of this imagined judge. Apply this to yourself, and it turns out that the question is not only "how do I look" but also "whose eyes am I looking at myself through". That gaze is usually assembled from advertising, other people's words, old remarks. Once you tell it apart from your own, you can loosen its power a little.
body_shame.practice: When you look in the mirror, ask: whose eyes am I looking at myself through right now — a magazine's, an old remark's, an imagined viewer's? Name that gaze and, in your mind, ask it to leave the room.

illness.text: A body that suddenly stops obeying is something Žižek, following Lacan, would call an intrusion of the Real — what doesn't fit into your usual picture of yourself and the world. When your body lets you down, it is both frightening and galling. Normally we live as if the body were an obedient instrument; illness reminds us that we are not entirely our own masters, and that knowledge hurts. At the same time, Žižek mocks "Western Buddhism" — the fashionable advice to keep your inner calm at any cost. It follows that you have the right to be angry, to be afraid, not to cope perfectly. Illness is not a defeat, nor a lesson that has to be learned "correctly". It is an event you can be honest with, without putting on a show of serenity.
illness.practice: Say out loud how you really are right now — without "but I'm holding up" at the end.

pride.text: "I did it" — and at once you want to add a "but": Žižek would say the insatiable superego adds that "but" for you. Pride in what you have done is a good, legitimate feeling. Žižek, criticizing a culture in which "Enjoy!" becomes an order, would note that today even the joy of success is easily poisoned by the demand for more — "it could have been better", "others have more". The superego, for Žižek, is insatiable: the more we do, the more it demands. Žižek would phrase it like this: healthy pride is a small gesture of disobedience to this voice: you allow yourself to say "I did it" without a "but" attached. Žižek values the concrete act — something that really changed something in the world, however little. Your pride is an acknowledgement of such an act. There's no need to hide it or play it down.
pride.practice: Say out loud: "I did it" — and stop at the full stop, without adding a "but." If the superego tries to add one, smile at it.

melancholy.text: In his essay "Melancholy and the Act," Žižek notes the melancholic's trick: treating a lack as a loss, as if one once owned what one never had. Gentle sadness is a quiet and deep feeling, and Žižek looks at it soberly. Such a trick makes it possible to keep a precious object at least as a lost one. For you this means: gentle sadness is a way of staying close to something that always slipped away a little, and there's nothing wrong with that. Žižek would warn against only one thing — turning it into a hiding place from the present. You can live through melancholy without giving up what is possible now.
melancholy.practice: Write down what your sadness is about. Then ask, as Žižek would: did I ever really have this — or is it what I always dreamed of?
